             SUDHIR S/O MOTIRAMJI HIWARKAR & ORS.                            … RESPONDENTS

             DIPANKAR DATTA, J.


             1. These civil appeals, by special leave granted on 11th March, 2016, are

                         directed against the judgment and order dated 7th October, 20151,

                         passed by the High Court of Judicature at Bombay, Bench at Nagpur 2,

                         allowing a writ petition3 of the first respondent4 as well as a subsequent

                         order of dismissal of a review application5 of the Joint Director of Higher

                         Education, Nagpur6, dated 12th January, 2016. While granting leave, the

                         direction contained in paragraph 26 (iv) of the impugned judgment was

                         stayed.

2. The factual matrix, confined to what is necessary for the disposal of the

    present appeals, is that Sudhir was appointed as a Lecturer in the

    Commerce Faculty of the third respondent7 (run by the second

    respondent8) in the academic session 1990-1991. The College was

    granted permission to operate strictly on a “no grant-in-aid” basis9.

    Following a series of earlier terminations and reinstatements, Sudhir was

    placed under suspension, and the Management of the Society initiated

    a departmental enquiry. Upon completion of the enquiry and after

    obtaining permission from the University, Sudhir was terminated from

    service on 17th August, 1999. Contemporaneously, the University also

    granted permission to the Management to close down the Commerce

    Faculty from the academic session 1999-2000 for want of students.

3. Sudhir challenged his termination before the University and College

    Tribunal, Nagpur10, which dismissed his appeal vide order dated 24th

    April, 2000. Aggrieved thereby, Sudhir filed a writ petition before the

    High Court. By the impugned judgment, the High Court set aside the

    order of the Tribunal and quashed the order of termination. Inter alia,

    the High Court directed the “Joint Director” to take steps to include

    Sudhir’s name in the list of surplus lecturers/teachers and to absorb him

    in any other college [paragraph 26 (iv)]. The High Court further directed

    the Management to pay a sum of Rs. 10,00,000/- (Rupees ten lakh) to

    Sudhir towards compensation in lieu of arrears. Aggrieved by the


7
  College
8

9
  Communication dated 21st July, 1990 addressed to Respondent No. 4 (University)
10
   Tribunal

                                     Page 2 of 8
      direction regarding absorption, the Joint Director filed a review

      application, which came to be dismissed as noted above.

4. We have accorded our thoughtful consideration to the rival submissions

      advanced by learned counsel appearing for the respective parties and

      have perused the materials on record.

5. On behalf of the appellant, it was primarily urged that the College was

      functioning entirely on a “no grant-in-aid” basis. Relying upon

      Government Resolution (G.R.) dated 24th March, 1994 and a subsequent

      corrigendum dated 21st March, 1997, it was submitted that the policy

      for the absorption of surplus lecturers/teachers is applicable exclusively

      to grant-in-aid colleges and that the High Court exceeded its jurisdiction

      in directing the absorption of Sudhir, quite contrary to law.

6. Per contra, learned counsel for Sudhir submitted that under Section

      79(4) of the Maharashtra Universities Act, 199411, the mandate to

      absorb surplus lecturers/teachers applies to all “affiliated colleges”

      without distinguishing between aided and unaided institutions, rendering

      the 1997 G.R. non-est in law. To claim parity, reliance has been placed

      on the absorption of another similarly situated lecturer, Bhaurao s/o

      Pundlikrao Kadav (since deceased).

7. Having considered the rival submissions, the fulcrum of the present

      dispute lies, notably, in a fundamental procedural infirmity that goes to

      the root of the matter: the non-impleadment of the State of Maharashtra

      in the writ proceedings before the High Court.



11
     Universities Act

                                    Page 3 of 8
8. It is an admitted position that the State of Maharashtra was not arrayed

      as a party respondent in the writ petition instituted by Sudhir. It was

      only in March 2015—nearly fifteen years after the institution of the writ

      petition—that Sudhir filed an application seeking impleadment of the

      “Joint Director” as the sixth respondent, and not the State eo nomine.

      The High Court proceeded to issue a writ of mandamus directing the

      inclusion of Sudhir in the list of surplus lecturers/teachers for his

      absorption—a      direction   that   unequivocally   fastens   a   direct   and

      continuous financial and administrative liability upon the State.

9. On behalf of Sudhir, it was contended that the writ petition was

      competent, since the State of Maharashtra was duly represented

      through the office of the Joint Director and the learned Assistant

      Government Pleader had contested the matter on merits. The

      contention, however, overlooks the settled position of law that the State,

      as the necessary party, should have been duly impleaded in the

      proceedings; mere representation through one of its officers cannot

      dispense with such impleadment. The law on the subject is no longer res

      integra. In Ranjeet Mal v. General Manager, Northern Railway12, a

      three-Judge Bench of this Court held that an employee of the Union

      cannot seek to enforce an order setting aside removal from service by

      merely impleading the General Manager. This Court categorically laid

      down that the Union of India is a necessary party, as any order passed

      would have to be enforced against the Union, not merely its servants.



12
     (1977) 1 SCC 484

                                       Page 4 of 8
10. This principle was reiterated in Jagtu v. Suraj Mal13, wherein this Court,

       reading Section 79 and Order 27 Rule 1 alongside Order 1 Rule 9 of the

       Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, held that where a declaration of rights is

       sought in respect of land belonging to the State, the State is a necessary

       party. In the absence of the State, the proceedings cannot continue, and

       the suit is not maintainable. Furthermore, in Chaman Lal v. State of

       Punjab14, this Court deprecated the practice of granting relief against

       the State exchequer when the State itself has not been formally

       impleaded. It was clarified that a decree erroneously passed in such a

       suit would not bind the State, even if it had attained finality.

11. The impleadment of an officer or a department, without formally

       arraying the State as a juristic entity under Article 300 of the

       Constitution,   renders   the   petition      fundamentally   defective   when

       substantive relief is sought against the public exchequer.

12. Applying the aforesaid established principles to the present case, the

       direction contained in paragraph 26 (iv) of the impugned judgment

       cannot be sustained. The belated impleadment of the “Joint Director”

       does not cure the fundamental defect of non-joinder of the State of

       Maharashtra. An officer or a department of the State cannot be equated

       with the State itself for the purposes of fastening sovereign or financial

       liability. The High Court thus grossly erred in fastening liability for

       absorption upon the appellant without its formal impleadment as a

       necessary party.


 13
      (2010) 13 SCC 769
 14
      (2014) 15 SCC 715

                                       Page 5 of 8
13. Even otherwise, on merits too, the claim of Sudhir for absorption cannot

    be sustained. The undisputed fact that Sudhir was appointed in a “no

    grant-in-aid” college, clearly places him outside the protective umbrella

    of the State’s surplus absorption policy as clarified in the corrigendum

    dated 21st March, 1997. Sudhir did not challenge this corrigendum.

    Without any challenge, reference to the Universities Act cannot aid

    Sudhir. To bypass this executive policy, Sudhir seeks parity with another

    lecturer, late Bhaurao, who was allegedly absorbed. However, as held by

    this Court in Chaman Lal (supra), Article 14 of the Constitution does

    not envisage negative equality. If an illegal or irregular benefit has been

    conferred upon a similarly situated person inadvertently or by mistake,

    it does not confer any legal right on others to claim the same relief to

    perpetuate an illegality.

14. The appeals, therefore, have to and must succeed.

15. However, despite the aforesaid legal position, we cannot remain

    oblivious to the peculiar equities of the present case. Having battled the

    sword of Damocles over his employment since 1993, Sudhir ultimately

    attained the age of superannuation on 30th November, 2025, during the

    pendency of these proceedings. Because of the order of stay, he could

    not reap the fruits of the reinstatement order passed by the High Court.

    He accepted the lump-sum compensation of Rs. 10,00,000/- (Rupees

    ten lakh) from the Management in lieu of arrears, perhaps on the

    expectation that he would be absorbed in service, as directed by the

    High Court. He remained out of employment since 1999. While the



                                   Page 6 of 8
    appellant is correct in its submission that the legal mandate for

    absorption does not apply to a “no grant-in-aid” college, leaving Sudhir

    destitute at this advanced stage of his life would result in a travesty of

    justice. Indeed, the appellant, too, shares a degree of blame for not

    raising the specific objection regarding its non-impleadment firmly at the

    earliest opportunity before the High Court.

16. Therefore, having regard to the larger scheme of things, we are of the

    view that Sudhir may not be left without any succour at the twilight of

    his life. At our request, recorded in the order dated 12th August, 2026,

    the appellant has placed on record a calculation chart setting out the

    arrears of salary which Sudhir would have been entitled to, had he

    continued to serve as a college lecturer during the period from 7 th

    October, 2015 to 30th November, 2025. The net amount, so calculated,

    is staggering.

17. Nonetheless, with a view to securing complete justice between the

    parties, we deem it appropriate to invoke our extraordinary jurisdiction

    under Article 142 of the Constitution and mould the relief.

18. While setting aside paragraph 26 (iv) of the impugned judgment, we

    direct the appellant-State to pay to Sudhir a consolidated sum of

    Rs. 10,00,000/- (Rupees ten lakh only), within a period of eight weeks

    from date, in full and final settlement of all his claims. The compensation

    already paid by the Management shall remain undisturbed. This direction

    is passed in the unique facts and circumstances of this case and shall

    not be treated as a precedent.



                                   Page 7 of 8
19. The appeals are allowed on the above terms.

20. Pending application(s), if any, shall also stand disposed of. Interim

   orders, if any, stand vacated. There shall be no order as to costs.

       (iii) the deceased was last seen in the company of the

       accused;

       (iv) the weapons of assault were recovered at the instance of

       the accused;

       explanation and, therefore, the chain of circumstances was

10. Before we set out to discuss the rival contentions and the

evidence on record, we must not be oblivious of the fact that this

is a case based entirely on circumstantial evidence. As to when on

strength of evidence circumstantial in nature conviction can be

lawfully sustained, the law is well settled - the circumstances from

which the conclusion of guilt is to be drawn should, in the first

instance, be fully established; these circumstances should be of a

definite tendency unerringly pointing towards the guilt of the

accused; the circumstances taken cumulatively should form a

chain so far complete that there is no escape from the conclusion

that within all human probability the crime was committed by the

accused; the circumstances should be consistent only with the

hypothesis regarding the guilt of the accused; and they must

exclude every possible hypothesis except the one to be proved.

Further, the circumstances from which the conclusion of guilt is

to be drawn should be fully established, meaning thereby that

they “must” or “should” and not “may be” established5.

10.1.               Besides, while dealing with a criminal trial, a court

must not be oblivious to the most fundamental principle of

criminal jurisprudence, which is, that the accused “must be” and

 6. Relevancy of facts forming part of same transaction.—Facts which, though not in issue, are so

Illustrations
(a) A is accused of the murder of B by beating him. Whatever was said or done by A or B or the by-
standers at the beating, or so shortly before or after it as to form part of the transaction, is a relevant
fact.
(b) A is accused of waging war against the 25[Government of India] by taking part in an armed

(c) A sues B for a libel contained in a letter forming part of a correspondence. Letters between the
parties relating to the subject out of which the libel arose, and forming part of the correspondence in
which it is contained, are relevant facts, though they do not contain the libel itself.

delivered to several intermediate persons successively. Each delivery is a relevant fact.
7. Facts which are the occasion, cause or effect of facts in issue.—Facts which are the occasion,
cause or effect, immediate or otherwise, of relevant facts, or facts in issue, or which constitute the
state of things under which they happened, or which afforded an opportunity for their occurrence or
transaction, are relevant.
Illustrations
(a) The question is, whether A robbed B.
The facts that, shortly before the robbery, B went to a fair with money in his possession, and that he
showed it, or mentioned the fact that he had it, to third persons, are relevant.
(b) The question is, whether A murdered B.
Marks on the ground, produced by a struggle at or near the place where the murder was committed,
are relevant facts.
(c) The question is, whether A poisoned B.
The state of B's health before the symptoms ascribed to poison, and habits of B, known to A, which
afforded an opportunity for the administration of poison, are relevant facts.
8. Motive, preparation and previous or subsequent conduct.—Any fact is relevant which shows or
constitutes a motive or preparation for any fact in issue or relevant fact.
The conduct of any party, or of any agent to any party, to any suit or proceeding, in reference to such
suit or proceeding, or in reference to any fact in issue therein or relevant thereto, and the conduct of
any person an offence against whom is the subject of any proceeding, is relevant, if such conduct
influences or is influenced by any fact in issue or relevant fact, and whether it was previous or
subsequent thereto.
Explanation 1.—The word “conduct” in this section does not include statements, unless those
statements accompany and explain acts other than statements; but this explanation is not to affect
the relevancy of statements under any other section of this Act.
Explanation 2.—When the conduct of any person is relevant, any statement made to him or in his
presence and hearing, which affects such conduct, is relevant.
Illustrations
(a) A is tried for the murder of B.
The facts that A murdered C, that B knew that A had murdered C, and that B had tried to extort
money from A by threatening to make his knowledge public, are relevant.
(b) A sues B upon a bond for the payment of money. B denies the making of the bond.
The fact that, at the time when the bond was alleged to be made, B required money for a particular
purpose, is relevant.
(c) A is tried for the murder of B by poison.
The fact that, before the death of B, A procured poison similar to that which was administered to B, is
relevant.
(d) The question is, whether a certain document is the will of A.
The facts that, not long before the date of the alleged will, A made inquiry into matters to which the
provisions of the alleged will relate, that he consulted vakils in reference to making the will, and that
he caused drafts of other wills to be prepared, of which he did not approve, are relevant.
(e) A is accused of a crime.
The facts that, either before, or at the time of, or after the alleged crime, A provided evidence which
would tend to give to the facts of the case an appearance favourable to himself, or that he destroyed or
concealed evidence, or prevented the presence or procured the absence of persons who might have
been witnesses, or suborned persons to give false evidence respecting it, are relevant.
(f) The question is, whether A robbed B.
The facts that, after B was robbed, C said in A's presence—“the police are coming to look for the man
who robbed B”, and that immediately afterwards A ran away, are relevant.
(g) The question is, whether A owes B rupees 10,000.
The facts that A asked C to lend him money, and that D said to C in A's presence and hearing—“I
advise you not to trust A, for he owes B 10,000 rupees,” and that A went away without making any
answer, are relevant facts.

       Conclusion

11. In conclusion, we are of the view that there is hardly any

evidence basis which the conviction of the accused could be

sustained.

12. Accordingly, we allow the appeal and set aside the conviction

of the appellant and acquit him of all the charges for which he had

been tried. The judgment and order of the High Court and the

Trial Court are set aside. The appellant is acquitted of the charges

for which he had been tried. He shall be released forthwith unless

wanted in any other case.
